text: The Digital Ceasefire & De-escalation Handbook provides a framework and language that Parties and mediators can use to negotiate and mediate Digital Operations in Armed Conflicts, Grey Zone Activities, and Internal Disturbances. All words that are capitalized in this Note to Users and in the Handbook are defined in the Definitions section of the Handbook.

The Handbook was drafted to reflect the increasing use of Digital technologies and capabilities by parties, ensuring that any Agreement binding Parties to cease or de-escalate prohibited acts, whether Digital or otherwise, can include language to address this reality.

The structure of this Handbook is modeled after and adapted from ceasefire Agreements, including provisions in sections titled Preamble; Entry into force; Prohibited Digital Operations; Third Parties; Constructive Digital Operations; Digital Monitoring Commission; Dissemination and Promotion of the Agreement; External Support; Definitions; and Signatories. Although ceasefire Agreements usually extend beyond International Law obligations, parties often acknowledge their legal responsibilities, so an Annex for Commitments to International Law is included, from which parties can draw language depending upon whether they are negotiating in the context of an Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activities, or Internal Disturbances.

The provisions in this Handbook are a menu of options, not a comprehensive model to be adopted in full. Parties may select, adapt, combine, or omit provisions according to the context, objectives, and scope of the situation. As outlined below, Agreements may take various forms: provisions may be incorporated into an Agreement that addresses the kinetic elements of a conflict, annexed to such an Agreement, or stand alone.
Prohibited Digital Operations

The Handbook uses the term Prohibited Digital Operations to refer to Digital Operations that the Parties agree to De-escalate or cease undertaking. The term is therefore defined by the commitments the Parties choose to include in their Agreement and may encompass Digital Operations in the context of an Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activities, or Internal Disturbances.

Importantly, describing an operation as “prohibited” under the Agreement does not imply that such operations are necessarily unlawful under International Law; rather, it reflects the specific restraints the Parties have agreed to observe. This may include Agreement to cease otherwise lawful Digital Operations as a measure of restraint, De-escalation, or confidence-building.

If Parties are unable to agree to prohibit Digital Operations, they view cessation as infeasible or undesirable, or they wish to actively limit but not comprehensively cease certain activities, they can instead agree to de-escalate Digital Operations. In that case, Parties could instead use the term “De-escalated Digital Operations” and language such as “reduce” or "mitigate" or “de-escalate” instead of “cease” or “stop” or “prohibit.” Parties could then set a numerical or percentage threshold for De-escalation or set a frequency-based, severity-based, or impact-based threshold. This Handbook is structured around Prohibited Digital Operations, but each provision in this Handbook can be adapted to instead focus on De-escalated Digital Operations.
Categories of Prohibited Digital Operations
This Handbook divides Prohibited Digital Operations into three categories as set out in Section 3:

1. Internet Interference, which the Parties may agree include Internet Shutdowns, Internet Infrastructure Attacks, Electronic Jamming, Third Party Internet Interference, and Humanitarian and Emergency Connectivity Disruptions;

2. Information Threats, which the Parties may agree include Misinformation and Disinformation, Manipulated Media, Inauthentic Behavior, Doxxing, Online Incitement to Violence, Hate Speech, Online Recruitment, Malicious Online Advertisements, Interference with Humanitarian Information and Data, Harassment of Journalists and Media, and Intimidating Diaspora;

3. Cyber Attacks, which the Parties may agree include Surveillance and Spyware, Hacking, Malware, Distributed Denial of Service Attacks, Phishing, Critical Infrastructure Attacks, and Weaponization of Digital Infrastructure and Systems.

As is typical of ceasefire Agreements, the Parties may agree to cease Prohibited Digital Operations against Military Objectives as well as Civilian Objects and Dual-Use Objects, even if not prohibited by International Law.

In addition to the categories of Prohibited Digital Operations, Section 5.0 provides an opportunity for the Parties to establish and agree upon a set of permissible or constructive commitments relating to connectivity, cyber defense, information dissemination, and other human rights and humanitarian protections.
Application of the Handbook to Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activities, and Internal Disturbances

In the context of an Armed Conflict, this Handbook contains model language that may be incorporated into a ceasefire Agreement, appended as an annex to a broader ceasefire Agreement, or used to negotiate a standalone Digital ceasefire Agreement. Handbook provisions may also be adapted for use in comprehensive peace Agreements or other Agreements negotiated during the conduct of hostilities or as part of a broader peace process.

In situations of Grey Zone Activities or Internal Disturbances, where there is no Armed Conflict present, Parties may similarly wish to restrain, reduce, or cease specified Digital Operations. However, while Digital Operations may be ceased in Armed Conflicts, Grey Zone Activities, and Internal Disturbances, a Ceasefire presupposes the existence of an Armed Conflict.

In the absence of Armed Conflict, Handbook provisions may instead be incorporated into other forms of Agreement, such as political Agreements, codes of conduct, or adopted as Confidence Building Measures (CBMs) aimed at cessation or De-escalation. They may also be drafted as memoranda of understanding, framework Agreements, or other shorter instruments focused on broad principles. This Handbook also includes provisions relevant to contexts which remain below the threshold of Armed Conflict. In such instances other forms of language will generally be more appropriate than ceasefire terminology.

Digital De-escalation or cessation may occur in Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activities, and Internal Disturbances, and may involve a reduction in the intensity, frequency, scope, or end to Digital Operations.
Practical Challenges to Negotiating and Monitoring Digital Operations

Negotiating Digital Operations presents practical and technical challenges, which may affect how Parties agree to and implement certain provisions in this Handbook. Drafting requires careful consideration of what is to be prohibited and tracked and how such monitoring mechanisms can be designed to ensure specific prohibitions together with effective monitoring (see Section 6 for monitoring commission guidance).

Parties may, for instance, be reluctant to accept extensive restrictions on their Digital capabilities, submit to external monitoring, or reveal their capabilities for safety and security reasons. This may result in an Agreement that does not address some of the Digital Operations causing the greatest harm.

Attribution presents a further challenge: purported breaches, particularly Cyber Attacks and Information Threats, may not be attributable to a Party with complete certainty, including where Proxy Actors are involved. This Handbook addresses these challenges by enabling Parties to negotiate the degree of certainty required or designate that responsibility to a Digital Monitoring Commission and providing alternative approaches where attribution is not possible.

Digital technologies and capabilities will continue to evolve. Parties should therefore consider drafting the Agreement with sufficient flexibility to encompass evolving contexts as well as new and emerging technologies and forms of Digital Operations that produce effects comparable to those addressed by its provisions, even where they are not expressly identified.
Cessation or De-escalation?

The complete cessation of Prohibited Digital Operations may not always be immediately achievable or verifiable. Unlike some kinetic activities, Digital Operations may continue through anonymous or unattributed actors, Third Parties, or activity beyond the direct control of the Parties. Parties should therefore consider defining what meaningful restraint and De-escalation would look like given the range of actors in the particular context.

Provisions can be tailored accordingly. If the goal is cessation, Parties may identify the specific sources or types of Prohibited Digital Operations to be addressed. They may also focus on new or context-specific actions, allowing commitments to evolve in response to new Prohibited Digital Operations identified by the Monitoring Commission. The Parties may decide to focus their negotiations on reducing or ceasing Digital Operations which produce the most harm, whether kinetic or otherwise, to civilians, vulnerable communities, public infrastructure and data, or the military.

These approaches can provide practical indicators of progress while preserving the ultimate goal of ending Prohibited Digital Operations. Parties may establish appropriate benchmarks, reporting periods, and methods of verification in the Agreement.
Standards of Restraint

The provisions in this Handbook often provide a high standard of restraint. Where Parties may be unwilling or unable to agree to a maximalist prohibition, they may wish to adopt narrower commitments aimed at reducing or De-escalating particular Digital Operations. For instance, Parties may agree to prohibit a certain scale of breaches rather than one-off breaches; to assess and report on the harmful effects of breaches rather than only the number and type of breaches; and to Digitally track and self-report their own breaches for public awareness.
Specificity to Context

Provisions in this Handbook are designed to be adaptable to any Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, and Internal Disturbance. Parties should consider drafting more targeted provisions by identifying specific forms of conduct, content, or narratives relevant to their context, and providing additional parameters, such as time, place, or actors, to more clearly define the Parties’ commitments. Parties may find certain provisions appropriate to end active fighting, while more may be longer term, normative items that are appropriate for a future Agreement.
Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Companies

Because Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Companies’ products and services may be used to facilitate or otherwise contribute to Cyber Attacks, Internet Interference, and Information Threats, ICT Companies often play a significant role in the Digital dimensions of Armed Conflicts, Grey Zone Activities, and Internal Disturbances without being formal Parties to the Agreement. While ICT Companies are often important stakeholders in efforts to reduce harm, establishing shared responsibilities and securing meaningful cooperation can be complex given their diverse mandates, business models, and regulatory obligations.

Some experts believe that in exceptional circumstances, an ICT Company may become a Party to an Armed Conflict, depending on its conduct and the applicable legal thresholds. Where an ICT Company is state-owned, Prohibited Digital Operations committed under the direction or control of that Party may be attributable to that Party, and therefore any such acts attributed to State-owned, State-controlled, or otherwise authorized ICT Companies breach Parties’ commitments under the Agreement.

This Handbook provides provisions that allow ICT Companies to commit to ending the use of their products and services in the commission of Prohibited Digital Operations; to contribute their services to monitoring the Agreement; and to be signatories to the Agreement.

ICT Companies can also adopt separate commitments or codes of conduct, or serve as implementation partners. Such commitments may be voluntary or legally binding, depending on the nature of the instrument. The Agreement should clearly identify the nature of these commitments and, where appropriate, the specific ICT Companies to which they apply.
Emerging Technologies

This is a forward-looking Handbook that is designed to provide Parties with language that can be included for current technologies, but the purpose of the Agreement is a cessation or De-escalation of the effects and consequences of Prohibited and De-escalated Digital Operations, regardless of the specific technology or system used. Accordingly, Parties may wish for the Agreement to apply, where relevant, to new and emerging technologies and forms of Digital Operations that produce effects comparable to those addressed by its provisions, even where such technologies or operations are not expressly identified or enumerated in the Agreement. In which case, Parties should include language to that effect.

The Handbook does not include a separate Prohibited Digital Operation focused on Artificial Intelligence (AI), recognizing that AI is regularly used in connection with Internet Interference, Information Threats, Cyber Attacks, and other Digital Operations addressed throughout the Handbook. As the use and capabilities of AI continue to grow, the Handbook treats AI as a cross-cutting technology rather than a distinct category of Prohibited Digital Operations.
International Law

Because ceasefire Agreements often reference and reaffirm the Parties’ obligations under International Law, the Handbook includes an Annex on Commitments to International Law in section 11. Its provisions may be incorporated into the Preamble, included throughout the Agreement, or retained as an Annex as set out here.

While the Handbook provisions draw upon existing International Law obligations, they also extend beyond it. Some provisions reflect legal obligations for the Parties (with the applicable legal basis set out in the footnotes), whereas others provide model commitments that Parties may voluntarily agree to adopt as part of a ceasefire or De-escalation Agreement, including commitments to refrain from conduct that would otherwise be lawful. Other provisions may contribute to the development of emerging norms or the progressive development of International Law.

The inclusion of a provision in the Handbook should not, by itself, be understood as indicating that the conduct it addresses is required or prohibited under existing International Law. At the same time, users should note that Parties remain subject to applicable International Law regardless of whether they sign an Agreement and the Parties cannot use the Agreement to contract out of their legal duties and obligations.

In situations of Armed Conflict, International Humanitarian Law (IHL) provides the specific legal framework governing the conduct of hostilities, while International Human Rights Law (IHL) continues to apply as relevant without overriding it. In situations of Grey Zone Activity or Internal Disturbance, where International Humanitarian Law does not apply, International Human Rights Law provides the primary applicable legal framework in addition to International Criminal Law (ICL) in narrow circumstances. Users should also be aware that the relationship between the bodies of law can be complex and at times difficult to navigate.

This Annex takes into consideration the International Law obligations applicable to a Party depending on the nature of the Party (e.g. a State Party or non-State Party) and the context under which the security challenge arises, including Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, or Internal Disturbances.
Kinetic and Digital Dimensions of Conflict

Digital and kinetic operations should not be understood as entirely separate spheres of conflict, given they often occur simultaneously and can be operationally integrated. For example, Cyber Attacks may precede or accompany a kinetic strike; Information Threats may support Military Objectives on the battlefield; and Internet Shutdowns may be enacted just following military strikes on a city.

Users should consider this relationship when negotiating and implementing a Digital ceasefire or De-escalation Agreement. Commitments to ceasing or de-escalating Digital Operations should not be interpreted or implemented in ways that facilitate, enable, or provide cover for prohibited kinetic activity, nor should restraint in one domain be exploited to intensify hostilities in another. For example, a Party should not use a cessation or reduction of Cyber Attacks to create an operational advantage for increased kinetic attacks, nor should a Party exploit restored communications, networks, or Digital Infrastructure to identify or attack opposing forces or civilians.

Equally, a kinetic attack should not be treated as justification for breaching commitments relating to Digital Operations. Where the Parties intend violations or developments in one domain to have consequences for commitments in another, those consequences should be expressly agreed rather than assumed.

Parties should therefore coordinate between Digital and broader ceasefire and De-escalation arrangements where both are present. This could be achieved through common implementation and monitoring mechanisms; procedures for addressing operations that combine Digital and kinetic elements; protections against exploiting restored Digital services or infrastructure for hostile purposes; and mechanisms for managing alleged violations without triggering reciprocal escalation across domains.

Ultimately, the purpose of an Agreement is cessation or De-escalation. An Agreement’s provisions should be interpreted and implemented in a manner that reduces opportunities for Parties to shift activities between Digital and kinetic means and prevents restraint in one domain from being exploited in another.
Freedom of Expression

Nothing in this Agreement should be interpreted or applied to unduly restrict lawful expression, including political speech, journalism, satire, or legitimate criticism. All provisions should be narrowly tailored and applied consistently with International Human Rights Law, including Article 19 of the ICCPR.
Background to this Handbook

The text of this Handbook is based on a combination of academic research, dozens of primary source interviews, and a review of historical and existing ceasefire and peace Agreements. Consultations with technical experts, diplomats, mediators, advisors, people on the ground in conflicts, and Parties currently or previously engaged in dialogue and mediation processes is ongoing to ensure that the provisions proposed directly meet the needs of existing conflict and security challenges.
The Handbook was developed with reference to the Public International Law and Policy Group’s Ceasefire Drafter’s Handbook.

The authors recommend that Parties using this Handbook engage with technical experts who understand the Digital dimensions of the security challenge, the technologies being used, and how such uses might be monitored and verified. The authors also recommend scoping the full range of acts, both Digital and non-Digital, so Parties can address both or complement existing negotiations. Finally, the authors recommend the Parties work with lawyers to understand which acts of the other Party are already prohibited by International Law.

For further information, guidance, or training the drafters of this Agreement are available and can be contacted: Brett Solomon ([brett@brettsolomon.info](mailto:brett@brettsolomon.info)) and Betsy Popken ([bpopken@berkeley.edu](mailto:bpopken@berkeley.edu)) of the [Digital Ceasefire Initiative](https://humanrights.berkeley.edu/projects/digital-ceasefire-initiative/) at the [Human Rights Center, UC Berkeley](https://humanrights.berkeley.edu/).

RECOGNIZING that the {{o-context}} includes both non-Digital and Digital dimensions;
COMMITTED to understanding the nature, scope, harm, and cause of Prohibited Digital Operations in the drafting and successful implementation of this Agreement;
RECOGNIZING that Prohibited Digital Operations can be carried out in the context of an Armed Conflict, in the Grey Zone, and in Internal Disturbances;
DETERMINED to address Prohibited Digital Operations that most harm civilians;
RECOGNIZING that there may be participants or stakeholders in the {{o-armed-conflict}} that are not Parties to this Agreement, yet critical to its success;

MINDFUL of the importance of reducing barriers to participation, including those related to geography, gender, language, and literacy, and of ensuring the meaningful inclusion and representation of relevant stakeholders in the drafting, implementation, and review of this Agreement;

RECOGNIZING that the actions, policies, services, and influence of Third Party actors including Proxy Actors, Cyber Mercenaries, Third Party States, Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Companies, and civil society organizations may affect the implementation, effectiveness, and outcomes of this Agreement;

COMMITTED to the De-escalation of the {{o-context}};
COMMITTED to upholding International Law and to promoting full respect for [International Humanitarian Law in the Armed Conflict,] International Criminal Law, and International Human Rights Law;^,^
EMPHASIZING that no provisions in this Agreement undermine or diminish each Party’s obligations under International Law;

RECOGNIZING that in situations of Armed Conflict, International Humanitarian Law constitutes the lex specialis governing the conduct of hostilities. International Human Rights Law continues to apply alongside International Humanitarian Law but does not override International Humanitarian Law protections specifically designed for Armed Conflicts. In situations of Grey Zone Activity or Internal Disturbance that do not amount to Armed Conflict, International Human Rights Law remains a primary applicable legal framework alongside other applicable rules of International Law, including the UN Charter, International Criminal Law, and relevant treaty and customary international law;

COMMITTED to protecting civilians, including respecting the rights of women, youth and Children, and addressing the needs of persons and groups who may be disproportionately affected, and to protecting civilian infrastructure and private and public property including cultural heritage;

RECOGNIZING that access to the internet and other means of information sharing and communication, Digital and otherwise, is essential to protecting rights and that people’s lives, security, and wellbeing rely upon that access, particularly during times of {{o-context}};
RECOGNIZING that the same rights that people have offline must also be protected and respected online;

APPRECIATING that the use of technologies and the technologies and methods used in {{o-context}} continue to evolve rapidly, and that technologies and methods not expressly referenced in this Agreement may nevertheless fall within its scope where their use is consistent with the activities or effects addressed herein, without prejudice to the ability of the Parties to amend this Agreement as necessary;

RECOGNIZING that empowering civilians through public digital literacy education and rights awareness is essential to nurturing a population's agency, enabling communities to identify Information Threats and supporting the successful implementation of this Agreement;

RECOGNIZING that the use of Artificial Intelligence in Prohibited Digital Operations may accelerate and amplify those operations, increase risks to civilians, and undermine human oversight and accountability, and Emphasizing the importance of ensuring that the development, deployment, and use of Artificial Intelligence remains subject to applicable International Law and meaningful human control;

OBSERVING that while not all Prohibited Digital Operations have an immediate or direct impact on civilians, there are often indirect impacts with secondary effects that cause harm, physical damage, or death;

RECOGNIZING the role of women as advocates of peace on and offline, as well as the heightened risks, danger, and insecurity that women face online due to the use of Digital means such as Deepfakes, as the subject of Misinformation and Disinformation, and as targets of Technology Facilitated Gender Based Violence (TFGBV);

RECOGNIZING that Digital harms impact intersectional identities differently – including but not limited to gender, class, religion, ability, ethnicity, sexual orientation, age, and migration status – and therefore an inclusive, context-specific approach is needed to address these harms;

The Parties agree to suspend all Prohibited Digital Operations for the duration of this Agreement, as further specified below:

Prohibited Digital Operations include attacks against civilians and Civilian Objects both of which are protected under International Humanitarian Law in Armed Conflict irrespective of this Agreement. This includes any operation intended to, or reasonably expected to, disable, disrupt, degrade, manipulate, or destroy civilian infrastructure, communications, or services.

Prohibited Digital Operations also include attacks against Military Objectives. This prohibition applies irrespective of whether such operations would otherwise be lawful under International Humanitarian Law in the context of Armed Conflict.

Parties shall not conduct Prohibited Digital Operations against Dual-Use objects that serve both civilian and military purposes. In cases of uncertainty as to whether an object is a Military Objective or Civilian Object, it shall be presumed to be civilian.

Parties shall refrain from conducting Prohibited Digital Operations, including Internet Interference, Information Threats, and Cyber Attacks, that disrupt, compromise, or unduly interfere with humanitarian operations, personnel, communications, Data, or systems, or that undermine humanitarian access, safety, neutrality, independence, impartiality, or acceptance.
The Parties agree that an Agreement to cease Internet Interference against another Party does not enable a Party or Proxy Actor to use, conduct, engage in, escalate, or initiate kinetic attacks.
No Party to this Agreement shall use, conduct, engage in, or initiate the following acts of Internet Interference:

The Parties shall not intentionally disrupt or shut down access to the internet, in whole or in part, including through bandwidth Throttling, deliberate reductions in network speeds or capacity, or efforts to disconnect the other Party from the global internet.

Parties shall refrain from taking any measures that result in Internet Shutdowns or disruption of internet services within the territories under their control, including occupied territories or in sovereign jurisdictions where they have the capacity to shut down or disrupt the internet. This includes any acts that would hinder access to online communications, humanitarian services, information sharing, public discourse, personal financial resources, or other essential services that rely on the internet.
If an Internet Shutdown is perpetrated, the Parties agree that they are responsible for restoring the network as quickly as possible.
The Parties agree that no Party to this Agreement shall damage or disrupt the Public Core or availability of the internet.

The Parties shall refrain from conducting Cyber Operations or physical attacks causing destruction, damage, or the seizure or disabling of communications infrastructure, including but not limited to internet exchange points, Data centers, undersea cables, satellite and space-based internet services, broadcast facilities, and telecommunications towers.

This prohibition applies to civilian, Dual-Use, and military communications infrastructure, including infrastructure that may otherwise constitute a Military Objective under International Humanitarian Law.
The Parties shall cease the disruption of internet routing, domain name systems, and traffic exchange mechanisms.

The Parties shall refrain from using legal, administrative, or other measures to restrict or prevent civilian access to the Internet, including by criminalizing or prohibiting the possession or use of internet access equipment, confiscating such equipment, penalizing persons for providing or facilitating internet access, or restricting the use of tools, including Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), that enable access to the Internet.

Parties shall protect civilian personnel engaged in the rollout, maintenance, restoration, or repair of ICT infrastructure and shall not attack, threaten, obstruct, or otherwise interfere with their work. Civilian personnel include cyber incident responders and other persons tasked with responding to and investigating security incidents.
Parties shall refrain from disrupting power systems where such disruption is intended to or can reasonably be expected to disable civilian ICT infrastructure.

Parties shall facilitate the safe and timely provision of fuel and other essential supplies necessary to operate, maintain, and restore civilian ICT infrastructure, including backup power systems and generators.

The Parties shall refrain from Electronic Jamming, signal interference, or other electromagnetic actions intended to disrupt, degrade, or deny access to communications networks or services, including radio, satellite, mobile, and internet connectivity.
Parties agree to resolving tensions resulting from unintended spectrum interference through technical negotiations between spectrum regulators.

The Parties shall not direct, support, or knowingly permit interference with internet availability by Third Parties, and shall take reasonable measures to prevent such interference from their territory or through infrastructure under their control. Where such interference originates from or is conducted through the territory or infrastructure of a Third State, the Parties shall use reasonable efforts to prevent or cease its interference.
Parties agree not to provide or facilitate Digital connectivity for the purpose of enabling Prohibited Digital Operations or to otherwise undermine the terms of this Agreement.

The Parties shall not disrupt, degrade, or otherwise interfere with the continued availability of internet and communications services necessary for humanitarian operations, medical services, emergency response, civilian warning systems, and access to essential public information and services.

The Parties shall refrain from using Artificial Intelligence systems to initiate, automate, coordinate, or facilitate Internet Interference prohibited under this Agreement, including Internet Shutdowns, the disruption of communications infrastructure, and the manipulation of network routing and access to essential Digital services.

No Information Threats provision in this Agreement shall be interpreted to restrict expression protected under International Human Rights Law, including Articles 19 and 20 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), including political, academic, or artistic speech, satire, journalism, debate, dissent, or criticism.
The Parties agree that an Agreement to cease Information Threats against another Party does not enable a Party or Proxy Actor to use, conduct, engage in, or initiate any other form of kinetic attack.
No Party to this Agreement shall use, conduct, engage in, or initiate the following acts of Information Threats:

All Parties agree to take reasonable steps to prevent creating false information which is then disseminated or amplified as Misinformation. Parties also agree to take reasonable steps to avoid creating, disseminating, or amplifying Disinformation or otherwise harmful forms of information, including through Proxy Actors, in ways that may escalate hostilities, incite violence, or undermine peace efforts.

Parties agree that content prohibited under this Agreement includes the fabrication or distortion of material facts, such as the announcement of a false humanitarian corridor or incorrect location of conflict zones – which may amount to perfidy, the deceptive impersonation or synthetic reproduction of the likenesses or voice of political or public officials or representatives of humanitarian organizations spreading false information, or the hostile manipulation of public perception against peace negotiators or peaceful protestors.

Parties agree that spreading distrust in the Parties to the Agreement, the negotiators of the Agreement, the process that developed the Agreement, and the Digital Monitoring Commission is prohibited under this Agreement.

Parties agree not to create, distribute, or endorse manipulated or synthetic media, such as Deep Fake photographs, audio, images, and video, where there is a risk of it leading to or inciting violence or undermining peace efforts. This provision expressly prohibits content that leads to or incites Technology-facilitated Gender Based Violence.

Parties shall not knowingly disseminate or amplify authentic media presented in a false or misleading context, including media from other conflicts or earlier events, where its presentation is intended or reasonably likely to mislead affected communities and create a risk of inciting violence or undermining peace efforts.

Parties shall not create, deploy, coordinate, or support fake accounts, automated bot networks, troll farms, synthetic identities, impersonation campaigns, or other forms of coordinated inauthentic behaviour intended to manipulate public discourse, deceive populations, impersonate persons or organizations, suppress participation, or undermine the peace process.

Parties shall refrain from using coordinated or deceptive means to manipulate social media platform algorithms, recommendation systems, engagement metrics, or other Digital systems in order to artificially amplify deceptive, divisive, or violent content, or to distort the visibility, reach, or credibility of information online.
Parties agree to refrain from engaging in, facilitating, or enabling Doxxing of individuals, including civilians, or groups in a manner that endangers their safety, privacy, or well-being.

Parties agree to refrain from exposing any personally identifying details of civilians, journalists, humanitarian workers, conflict mediators, peace negotiators, Parties, or other agreed persons in ways that could lead to harassment, intimidation, persecution, or physical harm.

All Parties shall refrain from engaging in or facilitating Online Incitement to Violence, including any form of online harassment, intimidation, provocation, or hatred toward any person or group of persons for their beliefs that has a reasonable likelihood of leading to violence. This prohibition includes false, unfounded, unsubstantiated, or politically-motivated accusations of apostasy, treason, Terrorism, or any other similar charges.

The Parties understand that the Rabat six-part threshold test to evaluate whether content rises to Online Incitement to Violence includes an assessment of the context, the speaker, the intent, the content, the extent, and the likelihood of harm.

Parties shall refrain from posting or otherwise sharing content that fuels regionalist, racial, ethnic, sectarian, or tribal divisions that could threaten the peace, including content that targets specific individuals, such as peace negotiators and mediators.
Parties agree they will not use social media and communications platforms as tools for violence, radicalization, or societal unrest.
Parties agree to work, if possible, with social media and communications platforms to detect and remove content that may be in breach of this Agreement.

The Parties shall take particular care to prevent Online Incitement to Violence that targets, exploits, recruits, or otherwise places young people and Children at heightened risk, including students, activists, and peacebuilders.

All Parties shall refrain from creating, drafting, disseminating, promoting, or endorsing Hate Speech that incites, or has a reasonable probability to incite, discrimination, hostility, or violence. This prohibition extends to public statements, media, broadcast, and social media and communications platforms, as well as Hate Speech in the form of text, visuals, audio, and audiovisuals, including symbols, slogans, or imagery.

Parties agree not to engage in Online Recruitment or encouragement of Cyber Mercenaries, hacktivist groups, Terrorist Organizations, Child soldiers, Children, Criminal Organizations, or other Third Parties for the purpose of conducting, facilitating, or supporting Prohibited Digital Operations under this Agreement. The Parties understand that Online Recruitment also includes tacit encouragement such as directly implying there will be no repercussions rather than direct recruitment.

Parties agree not to pay for, sponsor, or otherwise promote Online Advertisements that spread Misinformation or Disinformation, constitute propaganda for war, incite violence or hostility, promote or glorify Armed Conflict, or otherwise undermine trust between the Parties, such as encouraging attacks on or blockages of humanitarian aid or inciting ethnic cleansing.

The Parties shall not interfere with, manipulate, falsify, or unduly access information or Data relating to humanitarian operations, including information or Data concerning civilians, aid delivery, or humanitarian personnel and missions. Parties shall refrain from undermining humanitarian neutrality, independence, impartiality, or acceptance among affected populations.

The Parties shall not disclose, transfer, or otherwise share humanitarian Data, including personally identifiable information, with Third Parties where they know or reasonably should know that such Data may be used to harm civilians.

The Parties shall not harass, intimidate, or conduct Disinformation campaigns against journalists, media organizations, or news platforms. This prohibition also applies where such actions are conducted against or through State-controlled, State-directed, or State-supported media.

The Parties shall refrain from intimidating, censoring, threatening, or taking punitive measures against members of diaspora communities, including where such persons reside outside their country of origin.
The Parties shall refrain from using Artificial Intelligence systems to generate, manipulate, disseminate, or amplify Information Threats, as defined in this Agreement.

The Parties agree that a commitment to cease Cyber Attacks against another Party shall not be interpreted as authorizing, permitting, justifying, or otherwise providing a basis for the use of any other form of kinetic attacks by any Party or Proxy Actor.
No Party to this Agreement shall use, conduct, engage in, authorize, or initiate Cyber Attacks on the following persons or objects, or using the following means or methods:

The Parties shall refrain from conducting or facilitating unlawful or arbitrary Digital Surveillance activities, including the use or deployment of Spyware or other intrusive technologies that enable covert access to the devices, networks, communications, or Data of civilians, including humanitarian actors, journalists, human rights defenders, or other humanitarian personnel. This includes but is not limited to tracking mobile devices to listen to the conversations of journalists with sources and surveilling the email communications of humanitarian actors to disrupt their activities.

The Parties shall not conduct Digital Surveillance, such as the use of Spyware, against civilians, journalists, humanitarian workers, or peace negotiators, including their own populations, except pursuant to lawful authority consistent with International Human Rights Law, and in accordance with the principles of legality, necessity, non-discrimination, proportionality, reasonableness, and in accordance with applicable International Law, including human rights, and with effective oversight.

The Parties shall refrain from using social media and communications platforms to track, target, intimidate, or otherwise take punitive action against dissenting or critical individuals on the basis of political views or other protected expression online.

The Parties reaffirm their obligation to respect the right to privacy, and shall refrain from interfering with the privacy of individuals within and beyond their territory in accordance with applicable International Law.

Parties agree to refrain from conducting or facilitating cyber intrusions, Hacking, or other forms of unauthorized access to penetrate official or personal computer network, system, or digital device of civil society, women’s groups, human rights defenders, community leaders, peace negotiators, and other individuals or groups targeted for their identity, role, or perceived affiliation, as well as the general public.

Parties shall refrain from accessing, exfiltrating, manipulating, corrupting, poisoning, falsifying, deleting, or otherwise compromising the availability, integrity, or reliability of Data belonging to civilians, humanitarian personnel or entities, or public institutions. This includes civil and administrative Data and systems, including electoral records, population registries, civil documentation, social security records, and other Data essential to the provision of civilian services.

The Parties shall refrain from conducting or facilitating Cyber Operations against the military systems, networks, communications, or devices of other Parties that are intended to, or reasonably could be expected to, disrupt, degrade, manipulate, or impair the functioning, reliability, or control of such systems.

Parties agree to refrain from Hack Back operations against Digital systems outside their control, including in response to an actual or suspected Cyber Operation. This does not prevent defensive measures undertaken within systems under a Party’s control.

Parties agree to refrain from deploying, distributing, transferring, or utilizing Malware, or any comparable or related tools, including ransomware and other extortion-based Cyber Operations, to infiltrate, compromise, or disrupt the integrity, security, or functionality of any computer or Digital systems, networks, or Data belonging to or affecting other Parties to the Agreement, civil society organizations, human rights defenders, and humanitarian organizations.

Parties agree to refrain from testing Malware with the exception of testing in isolated environments solely for the purpose of defensive analysis or removal. The Parties understand that for certain types of Malware analysis, such as correctly responding to a Domain Name System query, a limited set of network access may be required, but they agree to otherwise limit interconnectivity.

This Malware prohibition extends to attacks on civilians, the general public, journalists, media organizations, civil society actors, humanitarian personnel, political actors, peace negotiators, or individuals targeted on the basis of their identity.

All Parties agree not to conduct, support, or knowingly facilitate any Denial of Service or Distributed Denial of Service Attacks against the computer systems, networks, services, websites, or critical infrastructure of another Party. This prohibition includes any actions intended to shut down, interrupt, disrupt, degrade, destroy, or render unavailable essential services and communications, Digital Infrastructure, Critical Infrastructure, websites, and social media and communications platforms used by the public and Parties to the Agreement.
Parties agree that Phishing to obtain sensitive and private Data and information about another Party, including actors involved in peace negotiations, is prohibited.

Parties shall refrain from conducting Prohibited Digital Operations that disrupt, damage, disable, degrade, manipulate, or otherwise compromise civilian Critical Infrastructure or its operation, including infrastructure supporting essential public and civilian services.

Parties shall not weaponize Digital Infrastructure, social media and communications platforms, AI systems, or commercial technologies in ways that cause or facilitate harm to civilians or Civilian Objects, or undermine their access to essential services. This may include the use of such technologies for mass Surveillance, AI-enabled targeting, algorithmic discrimination, systematic content suppression, Digital financial exclusion, or the denial or disruption of access to essential Digital services.

The Parties shall refrain from developing, deploying, directing, or facilitating Artificial Intelligence systems, including autonomous AI agents, to conduct, coordinate, or amplify Cyber Attacks, as defined in this Agreement.
The Parties shall not use Proxy Actors to undertake or circumvent any prohibition contained in this Agreement.

The Parties agree not to finance, equip, train, or otherwise support Proxy Actors to conduct Prohibited Digital Operations and will take all reasonable, lawful, and appropriate steps to prevent and cease Prohibited Digital Operations by Proxy Actors. The Parties agree not to enable or tolerate infrastructure access for Proxy Actors.

Parties shall bear responsibility for breaches of this Agreement committed by Proxy Actors over which each Party exercises {{o-effective-control}}. This responsibility applies regardless of the territory from which the Prohibited Digital Operations are carried out. The Parties agree that the Digital Monitoring Commission shall be responsible for determining whether a Party has {{o-effective-control}} of a Proxy Actor.

Parties agree they have {{o-effective-control-of-a}} if the Party provided financial or technical support to the group [within 90 days preceding the Prohibited Digital Operation]; if the Party’s infrastructure was knowingly made available to conduct the Prohibited Digital Operation; or if the Party had advance knowledge of the planned Prohibited Digital Operation and failed to take reasonable preventive measures.

The Parties commit to exercising control over the following Proxy Actors to prevent their commission of Prohibited Digital Operations under the terms of this Agreement: [Proxy Actor 1]; [Proxy Actor 2]; [Proxy Actor 3].

Each Party shall disclose to the Monitoring Commission all Proxy Actors known to be acting on its behalf or under its control within [30 days of signature of this Agreement] and shall notify the Commission of material changes thereafter.

The Parties shall not direct, sponsor, support, facilitate, or otherwise coordinate with Cyber Mercenaries or other non-State cyber actors to conduct or engage in Prohibited Digital Operations in violation of this Agreement.
The Parties shall not request, direct, encourage, or knowingly facilitate a Third Party State to conduct Prohibited Digital Operations or otherwise circumvent this Agreement.

The Parties shall take steps to prevent Third Party States from engaging in Prohibited Digital Operations by using diplomatic pressure, applying economic sanctions, and restricting access to financial, technological, or other resources that facilitate such operations.

The Parties agree to take reasonable measures, within their capabilities and authorities, to prevent, discourage, or mitigate activities by Third Party States that could undermine the implementation or objectives of this Agreement. Nothing in this provision shall be interpreted as requiring a Party to guarantee the conduct of actors that are not under its direction or effective control.
The Parties agree to request the support of Third Party States in implementing this Agreement and abiding by their commitments under this Agreement.

The Parties agree not to direct, request, sponsor, support, encourage, or otherwise seek to cause Information and Communications Technology Companies, including social media and communications platforms, satellite operators, cloud service providers, AI companies, or other Digital Infrastructure providers, to engage in Prohibited Digital Operations. The Parties shall also refrain from knowingly using products or services provided by such entities for the purpose of conducting Prohibited Digital Operations.

The Parties call upon [ICT Company 1], [ICT Company 2], [ICT Company 3] to sign this Agreement. Where ICT companies are signatories to the Agreement, they commit to complying with the provisions of the Agreement.

The Parties call on the following Information and Communications Technology Companies, including social media platforms, telecommunications companies, and cybersecurity companies to {{o-commit-to-a-set}} to be developed in collaboration with {{o-the-mediator}}: [ICT Company 1], [ICT Company 2] [ICT Company 3].

The Parties agree that the purposes underlying Constructive Digital Operations are to mitigate the effects of the {{o-context}} on civilians and affected areas, to mobilize public support for Digital Peace, to encourage Confidence Building Measures by the Parties, and to ensure compliance with the terms of this Agreement.
The Parties agree to the following Constructive Digital Operations:

Ensuring the continuity of internet connectivity as essential civilian infrastructure. This means that populations are connected to an open and reliable internet, able to access life saving information and emergency services online including humanitarian coordination, emergency medical response, family reunification, and financial services, and that internet users’ rights are respected online and offline.

Publishing online content or media that supports and enables humanitarian services, access to aid, and the facilitation of life-saving information such as the location of safe zones and humanitarian corridors, including from the United Nations, international humanitarian organizations, and civil society organizations.
Supporting media stories and social media posts that endorse an end to violence and the achievement of peaceful solutions, and spread a message of De-escalation and tolerance.

Cooperating to maintain or restore interoperable Digital services and infrastructure necessary for civilian life, humanitarian operations, and the implementation of this Agreement. This includes harmonizing technical standards across borders and between Parties, for example by standardizing spectrum, television signals, and other forms of Digital broadcasting.

.Leveraging technologies to enhance and facilitate communication between the Parties, Third Parties, and the public for notification, deconfliction, incident response, and the prevention or resolution of misunderstandings and unintended escalation and to provide officials with essential Data and information to support the implementation of this Agreement.

Implementing strictly defensive cybersecurity measures to protect systems, networks, and Data from unauthorized access and disruption, and taking action to reverse threats, including notifying the other Party of previously completed deployment operations and removing Malware already implanted in the other Party’s networks.
Using Digital technologies to support early warning, emergency response, humanitarian deconfliction, and the protection of civilians from imminent harm.

Providing advance notification to the other Party and other Third Parties, for instance software vendors developing the relevant software, where appropriate, of Digital Operations, maintenance, testing, or changes to networks or infrastructure that could reasonably be mistaken for a Prohibited Digital Operation or affect the other Party; and to responsibly disclosing knowledge about vulnerabilities in the other Party’s hardware or software.

Undertaking activities to secure, repair, or restore critical Digital Infrastructure, including networks, Data systems, and essential services as quickly as possible in a way consistent with International Law and that preserves the right to privacy.

Sharing technical information necessary to prevent, contain, or mitigate Malware, vulnerabilities, cyber incidents, or other Digital threats that could cause harm to civilians or civilian infrastructure.
Securing, backing up, or restoring Data essential to humanitarian efforts and civilian life, including medical, identity, and other civilian records.
Using Digital technologies to identify missing or separated persons, restore family links, and facilitate the safe return or reunification of affected populations.
Undertaking Digital Confidence Building Measures that enhance transparency, reduce misperception, and enable communication.
Preserving Digital evidence relevant to violations of this Agreement or applicable International Law, subject to appropriate safeguards for privacy and security.

Seeking voluntary commitments from ICT Companies to support the Agreement and refrain from facilitating Prohibited Digital Operations, including through parallel Agreements, codes of conduct, or other voluntary mechanisms.
Taking steps to reduce malicious Cyber Attacks emanating from their territory.
Seeking commitments from ICT Companies to provide transparent information on the use of their products or services when a Party has breached a provision related to their industry.

Establishing an Incident Hotline between the Parties so harm can be mitigated through rapid interaction following a potential breach, particularly in the case of an error or misunderstanding. If necessary, the Parties agree to jointly appoint a Third Party intermediary to create a rapid communication mechanism that can resolve misunderstandings or clarify suspected violations before they escalate.
Other Permissible Digital Operations may be agreed upon by the Parties.
The Parties agree to a Monitoring Commission with the following composition:
The Parties agree that the following {{o-entity}} shall compose the Monitoring Commission: [entity 1]; [entity 2]; [entity 3].
The Parties agree that {{o-entity}} shall name a {{o-chairperson}} to oversee the Monitoring Commission.
The Parties agree that {{o-individual}} shall serve {{o-as-the-chairperson}} to oversee the Monitoring Commission.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission shall be responsible for determining what structure and personnel will best enable it to fulfill its roles.

The Parties understand that the Monitoring Commission may recruit representatives from non-profit organizations, academic institutions, local community leaders, civil society representatives, respected religious leaders, and Information and Communication Technology Companies to contribute to fulfilling the Monitoring Commission’s roles. Because local civil society organizations are often the first to detect Internet Shutdowns, document alleged breaches, verify breaches, and engage affected communities, they may be considered core monitoring partners.
The Parties agree to appoint their own representatives in the relevant sectors to respond to and collaborate with the Monitoring Commission.

The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission must have the ability to understand, read, speak, and write in local, tribal, or Indigenous languages and that resources should be provided to enable it to do so.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission must remain neutral and independent to ensure trust and confidence among different political, ethnic, religious, and sectarian groups.
The Parties agree to a Monitoring Commission with the following role(s):
The Parties are committed to sharing relevant, timely, and accurate information with the Monitoring Commission upon its request.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission will serve as an intermediary for information sharing between the Parties of evidence of potential and actual breaches to the Agreement.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may create a mechanism to share information regarding alleged or actual breaches of the Agreement with the public.

State Parties agree that their national telecommunications and Digital regulatory bodies will share with the Monitoring Commission, or provide upon its request, information regarding Internet Interference from their territories and Internet Interference committed by Proxy Actors.

State Parties agree that their national intelligence agencies will share with the Monitoring Commission, or provide upon its request, information regarding Information Threats from their territories and Information Threats committed by Proxy Actors.

State Parties agree that their Computer Emergency Response Teams (CERTS) and Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTS) will share with the Commission, or provide upon its request, technical information regarding potential Cyber Attacks from their territories and Cyber Attacks committed by Proxy Actors, but may avoid attributing Cyber Attacks to a particular Party or Proxy Actor.

State Parties agree that representatives from their [CERTS and CSIRTS], [national intelligence agencies], [and national telecommunications and Digital regulatory bodies] shall participate in the Monitoring Commission to better facilitate information sharing.
The Parties agree to share information on a timely basis and preserve the privacy of information shared with or by the Monitoring Commission or other Parties.
The Parties agree to Digitally track and self-report any potential breaches to the Agreement of their own to the Monitoring Commission.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may {{o-request}} that the Parties provide access to the Commission to {{o-certain-systems-to-allow}}.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for monitoring compliance with this Agreement.
The Parties agree that monitoring means observing and recording events or actions related to this Agreement without making formal judgments about the Parties’ compliance with this Agreement.

The Parties understand that the Monitoring Commission will monitor potential breaches of the Agreement to the extent possible, recognizing that the level of certainty will depend on the type of breach (Internet Interference, Information Threat, or Cyber Attack), the information available about the possible breach, the technical capacity of the monitors, and the good faith of the Parties in providing relevant information.

The Parties authorize the Monitoring Commission to establish a mechanism by which Parties and non-parties can safely and anonymously report potential breaches of this Agreement. Non-parties may include civil society organizations, independent experts, international actors, and affected civilians.
The Parties agree that the Commission shall be responsible for establishing a process and timeline to notify the Parties of any Party’s perceived breaches to the Agreement.

The Parties agree that as part of its responsibility to monitor breaches to the Agreement, the Commission may request that Information and Communication Technology Companies provide information designed to help monitor breaches. Such requests may include, but are not limited to, information on: Cyber Attacks using a company’s tools or infrastructure; a Party to the Agreement demanding the company enact an Internet Shutdown; a Party’s or Proxy Actor’s use of a social media or communications platform for Online Incitement to Violence. In the case of Information Threats, the Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may {{o-require}} that a social media or communications platform preserve evidence. The Monitoring Commission may also use Information and Telecommunications Companies products and services to help attribute and verify potential breaches to the Agreement.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may request the technical support of ICT Companies for the purposes of monitoring the Agreement.

The Parties agree that as part of its responsibility to monitor breaches to the Agreement, the Monitoring Commission may request that Third Party States provide evidence of breaches with the Commission.
The Parties call upon ICT Companies with evidence of breaches of this Agreement to share that evidence with the Monitoring Commission.
The Parties call on Third Party States with evidence of breaches of this Agreement, to share that evidence with the Monitoring Commission.
The Parties agree that as part of its responsibility to monitor breaches to the Agreement, the Commission may request cooperation from Third Parties including Third Party States and ICT Companies.
The Parties agree to monitor their own compliance with the Agreement and to notify the Monitoring Commission of their own potential breaches to its provisions.
The Parties agree that if necessary, the Monitoring Commission may investigate alleged breaches through other means (e.g. interviews, open source investigations).
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may monitor the scale of alleged breaches as opposed to or in addition to each individual breach.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may monitor the harms of Prohibited Digital Operations allegedly committed by the Parties as opposed to or in addition to the breaches themselves.

The Parties urge the Monitoring Commission to understand local languages for the purpose of monitoring Information Threats to be able to adequately understand and assess the drivers of violence and social tension.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for examining and verifying whether allegations of breaches reported to or observed by the Monitoring Commission are indeed breaches.

The Parties agree that examination and verification means assessing and confirming whether the Parties are complying with this Agreement based on information observed or obtained by the Monitoring Commission or provided to the Monitoring Commission.

The Parties understand that to address instances where the Monitoring Commission is unable to verify and attribute potential breaches with absolute certainty, the Monitoring Commission will set percentage confidence thresholds disclosed to the Parties in advance (e.g. 80%) for each potential type of breach (e.g. Distributed Denial of Service) to be attributed to a particular Party. The Parties understand this percentage confidence threshold is likely to vary based on whether the breach concerns Internet Interference, Information Threats, or Cyber Attacks, and based on the incident and information available, and that breaches are only attributable up to that threshold.

The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may use the products and services of Information and Telecommunications Companies to help attribute and verify potential breaches to the Agreement, where possible.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible, upon verifying a breach, for determining whether a Party, civilian, or other non-Party has legal or other recourse.

The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for reporting all verified breaches. The Parties understand this may result in a significant lag between an incident and a Commission finding, during which time the Parties shall refrain from publicly accusing one another.

The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for initially reporting all potential breaches to the Agreement. The Parties understand that reporting potential breaches may risk damaging a Party’s reputation before the Commission has confirmed the allegation, and the Parties shall not escalate their Prohibited Digital Operations before a Commission finding.

The Parties agree that reporting means sharing information about {{o-verified}} breaches of this Agreement with the public – using a structured, impartial, and evidence-based format that balances transparency, neutrality, and the protection of sensitive information. The Parties understand these reports are essential for documenting compliance, informing the public, and preventing escalation.
The Monitoring Commission may use Third Party evidence and Information and Communications Technology Company tools to report on {{o-verified}} breaches to the Agreement.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for reporting on the harms caused by Prohibited Digital Operations.

The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission will provide technical support and good offices to help resolve technical, operational, and political disputes between the Parties to this Agreement and provide best practices to the Parties.
If the Parties have questions about what constitutes a breach to the provisions of this Agreement, they can reach out to the Monitoring Commission for clarification.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission will hold consultations on grievances and concerns with the Parties [every six months]. The Parties agree to submit their allegations in advance.
The Parties agree that any Party can request that the Monitoring Commission suspend the Agreement if that Party believes another Party has materially breached the Agreement.

The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for determining and providing advance notice on the consequences for a Party’s breach to the Agreement. For instance, the Commission may require a Party’s appearance before guarantor States, communicate a formal statement of censure to the UN Secretary-General, issue a formal warning identifying the breach and requiring corrective action within a specified timeframe, or refer the Party for sanctions consideration.
The Parties agree that the announcement of this Agreement shall be disseminated by the Parties through command channels with written orders requiring compliance.

The Parties agree that the announcement of this Agreement and its provisions will be communicated to the civilian population in clear, accessible, and understandable formats, via print, radio, electronic media, social media, community networks, and all other possible means of communication. Announcements will be made in all relevant languages and translated as needed. Any significant updates to the Agreement made by the Parties must also be communicated.

The Parties agree to disseminate the announcement of this Agreement to all relevant Third Parties, including Proxy Actors, Third Party States, other States, and other actors who should be aware of the Agreement or may assist in monitoring the terms of the Agreement.

The Parties agree to communicate to their personnel, Proxy Actors, relevant Third Parties, the civilian population, civil society organizations, and the international community that the failure to comply with this Agreement is likely to result in renewed Prohibited Digital Operations and the breakdown of trust between the Parties and possibly violations of International Law.

The Parties agree to disseminate the announcement of this Agreement to and engage with Information and Communication Technology Companies and company Boards to promote compliance with and support for this Agreement.

The Parties shall provide accurate and up to date information concerning this Agreement to the media and shall not interfere with the dissemination of information about this Agreement. The Parties shall take steps to prevent dissemination of distorted or manipulated information about this Agreement.
The Parties shall give notice of this Agreement to the appropriate international and regional organizations.
